# Document Notes: Chapters 1-40

## Setting & Time
- **Time Period**: Spring (Ch. 1) through Winter of tenth year (Ch. 40)
- **Locations**: Multiple harbor towns, villages, and river crossings in unnamed region; Bruton Street (London residence); Caversham; Carbury Manor; Bryncombe (hill farms); Sheepstone Birches (copse near Sheep's Acre Farm); Bungay; Harrowmere; Beccles; Queen's Gate (London); Grosvenor Square (London); Abchurch Lane (London); Coldmere; Fengate; Elmford; Wilwick; Ostcombe; Mireton (river crossing); Yarlgate (river crossing); Braewick; Torcombe (harbor town); Harrowford; Kelmere (village); Larkford; Torhaven; Islington (London)

## Financial Transactions & Characters Involved
**The Money Crisis**:
- Miles Grendall incurred a debt
- Sir Felix was the immediate offender, paying with documents not legitimately his
- Herr Vossner initially wrote a cheque for the lords' portion but lacked sufficient funds at his banker's for Grendall's larger claim
- Second transaction: Document prepared where Miles Grendall undertook to pay Herr Vossner £450 at the end of three months
- Endorsers: the two lords, Sir Felix, and Paul Montague
- Herr Vossner produced £322 10s. in notes and gold in return
- Nidderdale and Montague met Fisker at the railway station; cost to each was slightly over £100

**South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company Share Issue**:
- Miles Grendall suggests to Felix about selling shares in the company (Ch. 23)
- Melmotte explains to Nidderdale that shares are "allocated" to directors but cannot be transferred until they "qualify" by putting in "a few thousand pounds"
- Sir Felix attempts to secure funds for shares (Ch. 27-28)
- Felix claims to Miles Grendall it is "absolutely essential" to take up shares tomorrow or Wednesday; states Melmotte said "the only objection about me and this girl of his is as to money"
- **Ch. 38**: Felix expressed particular anxiety to take up those shares
- **Ch. 39**: Dolly explained shares give 3% on money's worth while governor pays 6% and he pays 25% on borrowed money; shares ought to be sold; Melmotte knows all about it; Dolly will go to city with Felix to make arrangements; Melmotte will advance £1,000

## Key Characters

**Fisker**: American visitor, partner of Montague. Manners disliked by locals. Left for Frisco/San Francisco on Saturday, 19th April morning. **Ch. 31**: Large man of the day in San Francisco when he departed

**Paul Montague**: Fisker's partner. Invited to Carbury Manor by Roger Carbury for special week, later asked not to come due to Henrietta's visit. Present at Sunday night gambling assembly (Ch. 28); observed losing heavily to Miles Grendall at loo. **Ch. 31**: Met a woman from his past in Bryncombe hill farms in autumn of eighth year; she had crossed Atlantic to see him; he had seen her in New York on second journey to San Francisco and renewed promises; had previously explained engagement must end via letters; she claimed to have been faithful and recovered her own fortune from robbers; stated she could not reach San Francisco as promised and that he had quarrelled with uncle and returned; he felt his position embarrassing and odious; resolved internally that she would never be his wife and intended to marry Henrietta Carbury instead but did not know how to tell her with proper courtesy; his uncle was buying a villa for seventy-four thousand dollars in San Francisco. **Ch. 32-34**: Engaged in relationship with Mrs. Hurtle (widow). **Ch. 32**: Formed his own opinions about Melmotte; though connected with him, believed the Grand Director to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived." **Ch. 33**: Mrs. Hurtle confronted him about breaking engagement; accused him of loving another woman (Hetta Carbury); she had come from California to see him; revealed she had shown his letters as proof of their engagement; he acknowledged his position was indefensible. **Ch. 34**: At river crossing at Yarlgate, Mrs. Hurtle continued confrontation; revealed she had informed Hetta Carbury that she was Paul's promised wife and connected with Melmotte and the American railway. She had stated she was not ashamed to have this advertised; offered to show Hetta his letters if doubted; claimed she had given up every friend to follow him; asked if he had made same promise to Hetta; position required thought; uncertain whether immediate duty was to denounce lady he had ill-used. **Ch. 35**: Received letter from Mrs. Hurtle; she referenced their journey from San Francisco to London; claimed her whole life was at stake; stated her devotion separated her from everything; said she scorn to come as suppliant but wished him to hear her; acknowledged man's constancy might not stand two years in absence but expected remembrance of past; accused him of sinning against her to utter destruction; stated she had given up every friend; noted regarding other lady she knows nothing of his passion. **Ch. 36**: Mrs. Hurtle wrote extensive letter stating she has fought battle about her property and won it; resolved to follow him to England as soon as circumstances permitted; determined not to be beaten by fraud and not to plead as pauper; stated both had some property but neither could enjoy it; claimed she has made her way through difficulties; proposed their affairs be made one; stated she came to England alone; expressed she has had great struggle and cruel things said of her; claimed to have come without trunk of introductions or scores of friends; appealed to him to release her from misery of solitude; noted her nature is social and not melancholy; requested he see her as he used to, let them be cheerful together, dine together, take her to theatre; stated if he wished she would promise not to allude to his revelation though it is nearer to her heart than any other matter; suggested her woman's vanity makes her think if he would only see her again he would think of her as he used to; her thoughts were consumed with determination that he should marry her or the world should hear the story of his perjury; she did not yet have plan of revenge formed but thoughts could not be kept from it; questioned if she, with all her intellectual gifts as well as outward person, should be thrown over by a man she regarded as greatly inferior to herself; maintained he had promised to marry her. **Ch. 37**: In spring of tenth year, Paul felt surrounded by difficulties upon reading her letter; his heart was all the other way; felt there was no escape from troubles; could not contradict single word in her letter; he had loved her and promised to make her his wife and had determined to break word because she was enveloped in dangerous mystery; had so resolved before ever seeing Hetta Carbury, having been made to believe by Roger Carbury that marriage with unknown American woman would be step to ruin; Roger had said woman was adventuress, might never have had husband, might at moment have several, might be overwhelmed with debt, might be anything bad, dangerous, abominable; all Paul heard at San Francisco substantiated Roger's views; Roger had said to him "Any scrape is better than that scrape"; Paul believed his Mentor with double faith as soon as he saw Hetta Carbury; could not confide in Roger Carbury as Roger was his rival; would be for Roger's interest that Paul marry widow; knew Roger too honest to be guided by such feeling but still could not tell him everything; could not speak of Hetta to his rival; had no other friend to confide in except Hetta herself; thought moment of writing stern true letter to woman telling her marriage impossible and he must abstain from her society; but remembered her solitude, her picture of herself in London without even acquaintance except himself; convinced himself impossible to leave her without seeing her; resolved to write to her; was thoroughly in love with Hetta Carbury and not in love with Mrs. Hurtle; would have given much of his golden prospects in American railway to have Mrs. Hurtle reconveyed to San Francisco; yet had delight in her presence. **Ch. 38**: In summer of tenth year, accompanied Mrs. Hurtle to Islington in London cab; she continued talking during whole journey; remarked London was immense but dirty; thought New York not so big but pleasanter; fancied Paris gem of gems among towns; stated she did not like Frenchmen and liked Englishmen better than Americans; fancied could never like English women; stated she hates buckram; likes good conduct, law, and religion if not forced down throat; hates what English women call propriety; claimed what they had been doing tonight is improper but not wicked; nearly over after evening, dreaded parting with her; knew he was in great peril and did not know how to escape; when pleasant hour passed and brought her back to door, did not know what to say; must make arrangement for future meeting; found theatre piece had poor acting; noted position described in play was so nearly her own he could say nothing; she had spoken on purpose, fighting her own battle, knowing her words would confuse him; remarked woman hides such tears, may be found crying unable to hide them but does not willingly let other woman see them

**Sir Felix Carbury**: Baronet, age 5-and-25, ruined. Made a Director of the South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Incapable of actual service. Son of Lady Carbury. **Ch. 10**: Smitten with Ruby Ruggles; took himself two miles out of way for appointment with her at Sheepstone Birches. Met Ruby in meadow near copse; described her as having beautiful oval face, rich brown colour, bright hair, lovely moustache. Made promises of love; probably cared little and carried on as "proper sort of thing for a young man to do." Within half hour grew weary—noted odour of patchouli unpleasant, flies troublesome, ground hard. Promised to see her again Tuesday morning at bottom of kitchen garden but resolved not to keep promise; intended to write and bid her come to London, sending money for journey. **Ch. 11**: Mother expressed joy at news of engagement to Marie Melmotte; called it "magnificent splendour." **Ch. 16**: At Caversham dinner, Lady Carbury arranged that Felix sit next to Marie. Questioned whether Marie would consent to run away with him; calculated that if he did so and she were not forgiven by Melmotte, he could not afford the expense and trouble. After dinner hardly spoke to her. **Ch. 24-25**: Has been in Grosvenor Square since return from Carbury. Received note from Marie at his club on Saturday: "Come on Sunday at half-past two. You will find papa after lunch." On Sunday at about three knocked at door in Grosvenor Square; intended to ask for Mr. Melmotte but courage failed at last moment; was shown to drawing-room where he found Madame Melmotte, Marie, Georgiana Longestaffe, and Lord Nidderdale. Marie indicated that everything was prepared and directed him to book-room where her father was. Found himself with Mr. Melmotte in book-room on Sunday afternoon; Melmotte initially thought Felix had come about railway business; believed Felix had come about marriage; felt he had not been received with good humour; said "I didn't mean to intrude, Mr. Melmotte"; Melmotte asked about Felix's property; Felix considered telling the truth but lacked courage; described his property as not large. **Ch. 26**: Felt checkmated after meeting with Melmotte; full of wrath at Melmotte's insolence. Believed game was over. Believed he could marry Marie; father confirmed it; believed Marie would stick to him and was in love with him. Recognized that Melmotte was "perhaps the greatest brute ever created." Could not stand up to Melmotte and cursed him. Walked down to club; was carried to Beargarden in cab. **Ch. 27-28**: At Sunday house dinner with Dolly Longestaffe, attempted to speak of his money; asked Dolly if he could cash I.O.U.'s tomorrow; told Miles Grendall it was "absolutely essential" to take up shares tomorrow or Wednesday. Attended Sunday night gambling in card-room at eleven. Doubted propriety of joining party with Miles Grendall who seemed liberated from obligation to pay, but saw no alternative gambling table. Tried business with Miles about shares before dinner in smoking-room with "unusual courtesy." Argued with Miles in smoking-room about unpaid debts of honour; Miles walked away to invite others to billiards. Sir Felix considered exposing transaction to room but feared Miles was more popular than himself. Played loo with Dolly, lords, Miles Grendall, and Paul Montague. Watched Miles's movement and behavior. Felt very cross about decision that Miles's paper could not be negotiated at table; doubted Miles would honor his pledge to apply winnings to I.O.U. redemption. **Ch. 29**: When he read Marie's love letter at his club on Monday afternoon in summer of eighth year, turned up his nose and shook his head. Thought if there were much of that kind of thing to be done, he could not go on with it, even though the marriage were certain and the money secure. Called Marie "infernal little ass" and crumpled letter up. **Ch. 38**: Had passed last two days in unendurable idleness; referred again to money which Dolly owed him, not making complaint or asking for immediate payment but explaining with air of importance that if commercial arrangement could be made, it might be serviceable to him at this moment; particularly anxious to take up those shares. **Ch. 39**: Said he would dine at the club but could not stay and play whist afterwards. Acceded willingly to Dolly's plan of visiting Abchurch Lane on following day. Had difficulty inducing Dolly to consent to early hour; Dolly suggested 4 P.M., Felix named noon, promised to call at Dolly's lodgings; split difference and agreed to start at two. Dined with Dolly, Miles Grendall at next table; Felix would not join conversation between Dolly and Grendall. Dolly asked if anything was up between Felix and Miles; Felix said no, that's not the reason, and promised to tell all in cab tomorrow. Left club declaring he would go to Grosvenor Square to see Marie Melmotte. When he came to house he would not go in; realized he could do nothing further till he got old Melmotte's consent and could best do that by showing he had money wherewith to buy shares in railway. Found note from Marie on return home at comparatively early hour. **Ch. 40**: Quite willing to marry Marie tomorrow on condition money properly arranged but not willing to go through much work in way of love-making with Marie Melmotte; in such business preferred Ruby Ruggles as companion

**Miles Grendall**: The impecunious one; lacks credit. Secretary at gambling house. **Ch. 28**: At Sunday night gambling, was least respected man in confraternity yet persistence led them to play loo instead of whist. Won heavily from Paul Montague. Had destroyed paper counters representing above £1,000 and received considerable ready money "which was quite a godsend to him." Moved his chair farther from Felix and closer to Dolly Longestaffe during play. When confronted by Felix about unpaid debts, made no answer and walked out of room to suggest billiards. Pledged his honour that when party broke up he would apply any money won to redemption of I.O.U.'s with regular percentage, but Felix doubted his sincerity. Continued smoking in silence during confrontation. **Ch. 39**: Dined alone at next table to Dolly and Felix; spoke frequently to Dolly but would not join in conversation with Felix; never addressed himself to Sir Felix

**Herr Vossner**: German, produced cheque and negotiated the formal agreement

**Lady Carbury**: Widow; mother of Sir Felix and Henrietta. Very soft, very handsome, and very winning in manner. Does not seek happiness in love and loveliness but in social distinction, literary fame, and money. Her great fears and hopes center on her son Felix. Author of "Criminal Queens." **Ch. 24**: Visited Felix's bedside a little before noon on Sunday, standing over him, urging him not to delay approaching Marie's father; said "My dear Felix, pray don't put it off; you don't know how many slips there may be between the cup and the lip"; expressed eagerness that he go formally to Marie's father to make his proposition

**The Melmotte Family**:
- **Mr. Melmotte**: Wealthy figure who has taken up old Longestaffe's affairs. Roger Carbury considers him "dirt in the gutter." Regarded as an adventurer and swindler. No one pretends he is a gentleman. **Ch. 25**: Accustomed to spend Sunday afternoons in book-room, usually with company of Lord Alfred Grendall; meditating on millions and arranging prices of money and funds for New York, Paris, and London Exchanges. Was waking from slumber when Felix entered, cigar in mouth. Immediately believed Felix had come about his share of railway plunder; resolved to be stern and rude; believed he had risen high enough to be condescending; thought he understood the game better than his colleagues; could trade on timidity, ignorance, or cupidity of colleagues; liked young associates because less timid and greedy than elders; noted he had been obliged to "buy" Lord Alfred. Anticipated no greater difficulty with Sir Felix than with Lord Nidderdale. **Ch. 26**: Puzzled by English system of titles and property descent; questioned Felix about his being heir to an Esquire despite being a baronet. **Ch. 32**: Paul Montague believed Melmotte to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived." **Ch. 39**: Will advance £1,000 to Felix/Dolly for railway shares; knows all about the money situation
- **Madame Melmotte**: **Ch. 30**: Met guests at breakfast; abandoned idea of having meal sent to her own room when she found she was not expected to breakfast with the master of the house. With her, Georgiana had to go out in carriage every day; could only go to parties which Madame Melmotte accompanied her to. Madame Melmotte was "very bad" but was silent and seemed to understand her guest was only her guest as a matter of business. Husband kept himself very much apart from her and other guests; met him only at dinner, and that not often. **Ch. 40**: Going to dine out at Duchess of Stevenage's with Mr. Melmotte and Marie; attending musical party afterwards at Lady Gamut's
- **Marie Melmotte**: Has timid face, eyes turned to ground, nervous twitching hands. Felix has been courting her. **Ch. 24**: Sent note to Felix at his club on Saturday: "Come on Sunday at half-past two. You will find papa after lunch." In drawing-room on Sunday with Madame Melmotte, Georgiana Longestaffe, and Lord Nidderdale; looked anxiously into Felix's face thinking he had already been with her father; contrived to be alone with Felix near window for a few seconds; told him "Papa is down-stairs in the book-room. Lord Alfred was told when he came that he was out"; directed him to ask the man to show him into the book-room; "It was evident to Sir Felix that everything was prepared for him." **Ch. 29**: Wrote a note to Felix in spring of eighth year. Content: does not know anything about money and doesn't care how much he has; says papa thinks only of money; thinks papa would give them money if they were married; told mamma of her intentions; mamma is always afraid; papa is cross to mamma sometimes more than to her; will try to tell papa but often hardly sees him all day; will not be afraid of him; will tell him on her word and honour she will never marry anyone except Felix; doesn't think he will beat her but will bear it if he does; knows papa beats mamma sometimes. **Ch. 30**: In summer of eighth year, intrusted letter to Didon together with little present of gloves and shoes, went down to breakfast. Madame Melmotte she had to endure and go out in carriage with daily. Could only go to parties Madame Melmotte accompanied her to. **Ch. 40**: Asking Felix why he doesn't come see her; says Mamma would say nothing if he came; Papa never in drawing-room; Georgiana Longestaffe here of course; people come in evenings; going to dine at Duchess of Stevenage's then to musical party at Lady Gamut's; Lord Nidderdale expected to be there but she doesn't like him and will take only the man she loves, meaning Felix; Georgiana angry because can't go out alone; wonders why Papa has Georgiana here; states they not going anywhere tomorrow evening so prays Felix will come; determined to be true to Felix; if Papa beat her to mummy would stick to him; Papa told her to take Lord Nidderdale then to refuse him then to take him again but she won't; says "And why haven't you written me something and sent it to Didon?"

**The Longestaffe Family**:
- **Mr. Longestaffe** (the squire): Owns properties at Pickering, Sussex, and Caversham. Dealing with Mr. Melmotte regarding financial affairs. Recently decided family will not return from Caversham to London this year. **Ch. 17-19**: Promised to take Georgiana back to London but broke this promise. Received letter from Georgiana on Monday morning demanding money to visit the Primeros in Queen's Gate, London or permission to be taken to town. **Ch. 20**: Response came the following morning through Lady Pomona; Lady Pomona informed Mr. Longestaffe that Mr. Melmotte's invitation was to be accepted. Georgiana to go up on the Friday following. **Ch. 30**: Letter from son fell upon Mr. Longestaffe at Caversham like thunderbolt. It was marvellous to him that his son should have been instigated to write a letter. The Melmottes must be very bad indeed,--worse than he had thought,--or their iniquities would not have brought about such energy. Passage which angered him most was that which told him that he ought to have taken his family back to town. This had come from his son, who had refused to do anything to help him in his difficulties. **Ch. 38**: Wants to sell Pickering; cannot sell without Dolly's consent; Melmotte wants to buy the place; talking of £50,000 over and above the debt upon it
- **Lady Pomona** (Mrs. Longestaffe): Wife. Issues invitations to dinner at Caversham
- **Georgiana Longestaffe**: Daughter. Reputed to have strongest head and sharpest tongue. Strongly protests against the Melmottes at Caversham. Refuses to tolerate year at Caversham. **Ch. 17-19**: Lost in passion at prospect of remaining in country; swore she would marry a London tradesman rather than stay at Caversham. Felt betrayed by her father's broken promise. **Ch. 20**: Received undated note inviting her to stay with Melmottes. **Ch. 24**: At Melmotte's house in Grosvenor Square on Sunday; Lord Nidderdale continuing flirtation with her in half whisper. **Ch. 30**: In summer of eighth year, Dolly Longestaffe called on her—an uncommon action. He came at very early hour, not much after noon, when it was his custom to be eating breakfast in bed. He declared at once to servant that he did not wish to see Madame Melmotte or any of the family; had called to see his sister. Was shown into separate room where Georgiana joined him. She complained to Dolly: "Oh, Dolly, it is impossible to make you understand. A man is so different. You can go just where you please, and do what you like. And if you're short of money, people will give you credit. And you can live by yourself, and all that sort of thing. How should you like to be shut up down at Caversham all the season?" **Ch. 40**: Here at Melmotte house; angry because she can't go out alone with them; told Marie she didn't understand being left alone; will go to musical party at Lady Gamut's; says she hates music; called "set-up thing" by Marie
- **Dolly Longestaffe** (Adolphus): Son. Has already impoverished himself through use of wealth. Refused to consent to sale of Pickering unless given half the produce at once. Has will of his own. **Ch. 22**: Gets drunk. **Ch. 27-28**: Present at Sunday house dinner and later Sunday night gambling in card-room at eleven. Felix asked him if he could cash I.O.U.'s for him. Miles Grendall sat next to him during loo and moved closer to him. **Ch. 30**: In summer of eighth year, called on his sister Georgiana at Melmotte's house at very early hour, not much after noon. **Ch. 38**: In summer of tenth year, Felix referred to money which Dolly owed him; Dolly explained he cannot pay if he hasn't got it; produced letter from lawyer received within last half hour, delivered at lodgings early in morning; his governor (father) wants to sell Pickering and Melmotte wants to buy it; his governor can't sell without Dolly and he's asked for half the plunder; knows what's what; his interest in property greater than his father's; property not much of place; talking of £50,000 over and above debt upon it; £25,000 would pay off what he owes on his own property and make him very square; from lawyer's letter supposes they're going to give in to his terms. **Ch. 39**: Suggested meeting Felix at club at 4 P.M.; Felix suggested noon and promised to call at lodgings; split difference and agreed to start at two; dined with Felix; spoke frequently to Miles Grendall but Felix would not join in conversation. Declared he would go with Felix to city to-morrow to make it straight about what Felix owes him; Melmotte will advance £1,000 then Felix can get shares; asked Felix if anything up between him and Miles; Felix said no, that's not the reason but promised to tell all in cab tomorrow. **Ch. 40**: Not wanting property to go to pieces; describes himself as lazy and can't get himself to go in for things as he ought; has feeling that he doesn't like family property going to pieces; a fellow oughtn't to let his family property go to pieces

**Roger Carbury**: Gentleman, took degree at Oxford, became a convert. Works as a priest. Has not a shilling beyond his clerical wages. In love with Henrietta Carbury. Considers Mr. Melmotte disreputable. Landlord of Mr. Ruggles and owner of Sheepstone Birches

**Henrietta Carbury**: Daughter of Lady Carbury. Roger Carbury is in love with her. Does not wish him to talk of love but would be happy if he treated her as friend without making love to him. **Ch. 31**: Paul Montague internally resolved to marry her instead of Mrs. Hurtle; did not know how to tell the woman with proper courtesy

**Father John Barham**: Beccles priest. Roman Catholic

**Ruby Ruggles**: Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion. Strong, healthy, tall, with will of her own. **Ch. 10**: Met Felix Carbury at Sheepstone Birches. Told herself after meeting Felix "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife" and "I'll never be nothing unless I'm that." Contrasted John Crumb with Sir Felix Carbury

**Mr. Ruggles**: Old man. Holds land on bishop's lease (Sheep's Acre Farm belonged to bishopric of Elmham). Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate, making him tenant of Roger Carbury

**Lord Nidderdale**: Nobility. Also courting Marie Melmotte for her money. **Ch. 28**: At Sunday night gambling; played loo with Sir Felix, Dolly Longestaffe, Miles Grendall, and Paul Montague. **Ch. 40**: Expected to be at Duchess of Stevenage's dinner; Marie doesn't like him

## Migrations & Population Changes (Chapters 20-40)

### Births (Chapters 24-40)
- **Ch. 24**: Riena Marrley gave birth to son named Cotho Quillson; father was Perald Quillson; family lived in Ostcombe
- **Ch. 25**: Felis Marrley gave birth to daughter named Molia Tallowley; father was Wedan Tallowley; family lived in Torcombe
- **Ch. 31**: A son was born to Felis Marrley and Wedan Tallowley, and they called the child Fenar Tallowley. The family lived in Torcombe
- **Ch. 34**: A son was born to Kanelle Quillick and Gamor Ashson, and they called the child Thibin Ashson. The family lived in Braewick
- **Ch. 38**: Dalis Holloway gave birth to a daughter, named Newyn Thornwood; father was Dadrek Thornwood; family lived in Ostcombe
- **Ch. 38**: Ridette Thornworth and Darald Thornwood had a daughter named Orlde Thornwood; family lived in Fengate
- **Ch. 40**: Voena Tallowenridge gave birth to a son, named Vodan Quillick; father was Codan Quillick; family lived in Wilwick

### Deaths (Chapters 20-40)
- **Ch. 20**: Ilbin Thornworth died of drowning in the flood at Kelmere
- **Ch. 21**: Vowyn died of a kick from a cart horse at Torcombe
- **Ch. 22**: Illan died of a long wasting sickness; laid in churchyard at Harrowford
- **Ch. 22**: Webin Ashson died of drowning in the flood; buried at Bryncombe
- **Ch. 28**: Nemor Marrley died of a fall from the mill loft; laid in churchyard at Mireton
- **Ch. 35**: Husband of Lurine Holloway died of the coughing sickness; laid in churchyard at Torhaven
- **Ch. 40**: Breric Tallowenridge died of a fall from the mill loft at Harrowford (Ch. 40, changed from Ch. 38 where he married)
- **Ch. 40**: Pelan Ashson died of a kick from a cart horse; laid in churchyard at Yarlgate

### Marriages (Chapters 20-40)
- **Ch. 21**: The eldest daughter of Lurine Holloway and Dadrek Thornwood were wed at Mireton; couple lived there from then on
- **Ch. 22**: Garic Quillson married Vorine Quillson in the chapel at Elmford; couple lived in Elmford from then on
- **Ch. 22**: Kanelle Quillick married Gamor in the chapel at Braewick; couple lived in Braewick from then on
- **Ch. 23**: Isssa took Nemor Marrley in marriage at Mireton; couple lived there from then on
- **Ch. 25**: Isnelle Thornwood took Vesmor Prydner in marriage at Torcombe; couple lived in Torcombe from then on
- **Ch. 30**: In the chapel at Mireton, Isssa Holloway married Netho Ashson. The couple lived in Mireton from then on
- **Ch. 31**: In the chapel at Bryncombe, Islis Ashson married Hadan Holloway. The couple lived in Bryncombe from then on
- **Ch. 32**: In the chapel at Elmford, Nelde Prydner married Rozek Thornwood. The couple lived in Elmford from then on
- **Ch. 33**: In the chapel at Elmford, Fetho Prydner married Rovie Tallowenridge. The couple lived in Elmford from then on
- **Ch. 37**: Before the summer was out, Tadette Prydner took Cotho Quillson in marriage at Elmford. The couple lived in Elmford from then on
- **Ch. 38**: Before the autumn was out, Ridette Thornworth took Darald Thornwood in marriage at Kelmere. The couple lived in Kelmere from then on. Ridette went along to live in Fengate as well. In the chapel at Larkford, Hara married Bredan Prydner. The couple lived in Larkford from then on.
- **Ch. 39**: Before the winter was out, Lurine Holloway took Breric Tallowenridge in marriage at Torhaven. The couple lived in Torhaven from then on. (Ch. 40 revised: Lurine Holloway rode out of Torhaven; by next market day she was living in Harrowford. Breric Tallowenridge followed her to Harrowford within the month.)

### Occupation Changes (Ch. 24-40)
- **Ch. 24**: Netho Ashson gave up being a miller and took work as a fisher
- **Ch. 26**: Isssa Holloway gave up being a herbalist and took work as a cooper
- **Ch. 31**: Bredan Prydner was apprenticed anew and became a miller
- **Ch. 35**: Darald Thornwood gave up idleness and took work as a shepherd
- **Ch. 36**: Ridette gave up being a tanner and took work as a cooper
- **Ch. 38**: Codan Quillick was apprenticed anew and became a miller
- **Ch. 39**: The second daughter of Ilbin Thornworth was apprenticed anew and became a chandler
- **Ch. 39**: The second daughter of Serine Marrley was apprenticed anew and became a chandler
- **Ch. 40**: Vodan Quillick bought a ribbon at the stall and then regretted it

## Secret Knowledge & Rumors (Updated through Ch. 40)
- **Tadrek Tallowley alone** carries knowledge that old abbey at Harrowmere hides second cellar (Ch. 1). **Ch. 6**: Confided location to Vorine Thornworth. **Ch. 31**: Vorine Thornworth could keep it no longer and told Pelan Ashson in river crossing at Yarlgate. **Ch. 34**: REVEALED—Vodette Thornworth burned letter from Vorine Thornworth revealing this secret

- **Breric Tallowenridge** carries knowledge that Thornwood mill ledger was rewritten after the flood (Ch. 1). **Ch. 20**: Told Riena Marrley. **Ch. 23**: Late one night told Perald Quillson. **Ch. 24**: Late one night told Ridette Thornworth. **Ch. 37**: Late one night in Harrowmere confided to Isssa that deed to Fengate pastures was forged. (Ch. 40: Breric died; Among things left by Breric, bone seal handed to Lurine)

## Legal & Customary Rules
- **Elmford Chapel Rule**: Vault beneath chapel opens only for living person who holds both garnet compass and brass mirror at once
- **Copper Ledger Succession**: By custom, copper ledger passes on death of holder to eldest living child; no will could change this; passes without ceremony
- **Fengate Toll Bridge Rule**: Toll bridge at Fengate belongs to Tallowley family; only those born a Tallowley or presently married to one allowed to cross
- **Sheep's Acre Farm**: Held on bishop's lease by Mr. Ruggles; belonged to bishopric of Elmham, set apart for its sustentation
- **Carbury Estate Land**: Mr. Ruggles holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate, making him tenant of Roger Carbury
